scores.strengths: Highest scientific value per unit of risk, and the only design whose survivability matches the citation lifetime of a paper. It is the only one that got the NTScore quantization domain right ([-8,0]; the measured minima are -7.688 utr3 / -7.281 utr5), and it ships the per-nucleotide track statically at a measured 33.9 MB — collapsing the single strongest argument the two server designs make for themselves. The caveat machinery is structural rather than decorative: gate bullet charts inline on every edge (not behind a toggle), a strict/suggestive tier control whose empty state is designed content, an entire /evidence view built on RAW_top30_annotated.csv's verdict column (25/30 ZNF artifacts) plus the Meff 2,342/18,068 arithmetic, and npmi_raw deliberately unavailable as a sort key without a warning. It is the only design that surfaces the contextual-embedding trap (34,110 unique_motif_ids in >1 cluster, 'CTGGA' in 176) as a first-class methods unit — a subtle correctness point that prevents a whole class of misreading. Its three-tier cluster naming, three-tier consensus fallback, and three distinct empty states mean no page in the 437-no-term / 434-no-PWM / 387-no-module gap regions is blank. Region `applies` masking is wired as a build-time regression test against the 8 published coverage numbers, not a UI filter.
scores.fatal_flaws: Does not answer the actual bilingual question for MY gene. The gene view shows three disconnected axes and, per selected motif, a 'top 3 partner clusters' preview — but never computes which protein-motif cluster PRESENT IN THIS TRANSCRIPT is gated-paired with which UTR cluster PRESENT IN THIS TRANSCRIPT. That intersection is the paper's entire thesis at gene scale, it is measured at mean 8.04 / median 2 pairs per transcript (65.2% of transcripts have >=1), and it is a ~1 KB static precompute. Its absence is the single largest scientific omission in an otherwise excellent design. Second, no arbitrary set query: 'which genes carry utr5_0079 AND prot_0072 but NOT ELAVL1' has no answer, so a reader cannot go past the questions the authors already asked. Third, it never found the mRNA-coordinate projection (cds_len == 3*prot_len+3 in 19,210/19,210), so the protein half stays visually severed from the RNA half. Fourth, it repeats the '7,784 nt model context cap' empty-state sentence, which is derived from `transcript_length` — a column measurably NOT the mRNA length (ACTB 1,059 vs true 1,812; shorter than utr5+cds+utr3 in all 19,210 rows). Shipping that sentence puts a false quantitative claim in the UI.

scores.strengths: Highest scientific ceiling of the four, and it is the only design that lets a reader ask a question the manuscript did not. The typed-AST Query Workbench over 541,746 (transcript, cluster) memberships with measured latencies (two-cluster intersection 3.4 ms, A AND B AND NOT C 28.8 ms, substring scan 11.7 ms) plus on-the-fly hypergeometric enrichment over a user-built set (13.2 ms, reproducing SLBP for utr3_0463) is genuine discovery infrastructure, not a feature. Refusing a raw-SQL box in favour of a pydantic discriminated union while still printing the compiled parameterized statement is the right call on both safety and transparency. It is the only design that engineered around its own worst risk: a deliberately three-legged release (live Cloud Run + DOI'd immutable Docker image + static export) so no single failure kills the citation. Its correctness fixes are in the CREATE TABLE rather than the UI — the MobiDB/IDPO/SignalP region leak fixed and verified to 0 rows, the 21,667->19,210 dedup, and the ID-bearing annotation rebuild that refuses to comma-split (wrong for 41.34% of InterPro / 6.894% of UniProt). Per-leaf cardinality badges before RUN are a real usability-for-science touch.
scores.fatal_flaws: Specifies a uint8 NTScore quantization over [-5, 0]. The measured minima are -7.688 (utr3) and -7.281 (utr5), so the most negative — i.e. most interesting, most model-surprising — nucleotides are silently clipped flat in the exact track that is the design's headline justification. That is a scientific error in the primary visual, not a rendering preference. Second, the workbench's enrichment runs on a transcript-level universe while the published table is gene-level, and the design's own benchmark returns SLBP k=23 / fold 51.5 against the paper's k=22 / fold 48.62. A portal whose flagship analytical feature disagrees with its own paper's numbers by default is a verification hazard; naming the universe in a caption is a mitigation, not a fix. Third, the archival leg is circular: the static export explicitly drops the workbench and the NTScore, i.e. exactly the two capabilities the backend existed to provide, so the permanent artifact is strictly worse than the static design's permanent artifact. Fourth, 42 dev-days of TypeScript/React/Vite/TanStack handed to a first-author computational biologist with zero package.json anywhere in the tree — the person who must patch this in year three cannot. Fifth, it shares static's blindness to in-transcript coupling and the mRNA projection.

scores.strengths: The best-argued framework evaluation of the four, and its decisive insight is correct and load-bearing: Dash renders html.Span into the real page DOM reachable by pattern-matching callbacks, so R1's clickable sequence needs zero custom React components — precisely where Streamlit's iframe abstraction breaks. Using Dash+Plotly because they are already installed and the author has already written 1,385 lines of Plotly interaction code is the right kind of pragmatism. It caught a real scientific bug nobody else did, by actually hitting it: keying the gene page on gene_symbol and taking sequence_id.iloc[0] silently mis-slices the 215 multi-transcript genes (APEX1's two transcripts have 232 vs 237 nt 5'UTRs), so motif coordinates from one address the other. That belongs in every build's assertion suite. Its memory measurements are the most careful of any design (153.3 MB slim frame, 352.6 MB with both indexes, 435.2 MB if annotations were resident — hence Tier B on disk), and its 0.27 ms in-RAM lookup vs DuckDB's 7.3 ms correctly kills the query-engine dependency for the read paths. Cluster-page region-conditionality (protein gets pLDDT, UTR gets none rather than an empty panel) is exactly right given 600 clusters have no pLDDT.
scores.fatal_flaws: Dominated on the cost/benefit frontier: it pays the full operational price of a live server — a process to run, patch, monitor, and fund; a cold start on a link printed in a paper; death when the VM is reclaimed — and collects almost none of the dividend. It explicitly declines to build an inverted index or any set-query capability, so unlike the backend it enables no question the manuscript did not already ask. Its stated static fallback is asserted in one sentence, never designed. Second, it concedes Plotly has no force layout, no edge bundling and no node dragging in dcc.Graph, and it never measured browser-side render time for 2,620 SVG edge segments — so R3, the view whose entire purpose is legible structure, will be the weakest of the four renderings, on a framework chosen for reasons unrelated to R3. Third, it sets the NTScore y-domain per transcript ('roughly -4.3..0, set per transcript'), which means two gene pages carry different y-axes and cross-gene comparison of the manuscript's central quantity is silently invalid. A fixed [-8,0] is required. Fourth, it inherits the same two blind spots as static and backend: no in-transcript coupling, no mRNA projection, and it repeats the false 7,784 nt cap.

scores.strengths: None. Every field is the literal string 'undefined': no stack, no architecture, zero views, zero viz units, no pipeline, no phases, no tradeoffs, no risks, no effort estimate. There is nothing to credit.
scores.fatal_flaws: The design does not exist. It cannot answer 'what motifs does my gene carry', cannot show a cluster, cannot render a module network, cannot carry the phylogenetic-independence caveat, and cannot be built. It contributes no idea worth grafting into a hybrid. Scoring it above zero at all only acknowledges that an empty slot is not actively harmful the way a misleading design would be. It should be excluded from the comparison rather than treated as a fourth option, and if the intent was a narrative/guided-tour angle, that angle remains genuinely unexplored — which is a loss, because a guided path through the ZNF-artifact story is the single most persuasive thing this portal could offer a reviewer.

reasoning:
Judged only on whether a reader can interrogate the bilingual motifome, verify manuscript claims, and learn something new about their own gene.

WHY [static] WINS. It scores highest on verification and on durability, which for a paper companion are the same axis: a portal that cannot be reached in 2031 has zero scientific value regardless of what it once did. It is the only design to get the NTScore quantization domain right, and — decisively — it MEASURED that the per-nucleotide track ships statically at 33.9 MB, which vaporizes the central argument both server designs make for their own existence. Its caveat machinery is structural rather than cosmetic: gate values inline on every edge rather than behind a toggle, an entire evidence view built on the authors' own 25/30 ZNF-artifact verdict table plus the Meff arithmetic, npmi_raw deliberately hard to sort by, non-significant results shown by default, and three-tier fallbacks so none of the 437-no-term / 434-no-PWM / 387-no-module pages is blank. It alone surfaced the unique_motif_id contextual-embedding trap, which is exactly the kind of subtle correctness point that separates a resource from a demo.

WHY IT IS ONLY 87 AND NOT HIGHER. It fails the brief's own last clause. "What motifs does MY gene carry and what do they pair with" has two halves; [static] answers the first completely and the second only generically — it shows the top partners of a clicked motif's cluster across the whole corpus, never the pairs actually co-present in the transcript on screen. That intersection is the paper's thesis at gene scale, it is mean 8.04 pairs per transcript, and it is a one-kilobyte static precompute. Nobody found it, and nobody found the mRNA projection that would let the protein and RNA halves share an axis. Those two omissions are why the hybrid is not simply "ship [static]".

WHY [backend] IS SECOND AT 80. It has the highest ceiling by a distance: the query workbench is the only feature in any design that lets a reader ask a question the manuscript did not ask, and its latencies are measured, not asserted. But two things cap it. Its own headline visual is specified with a [-5,0] quantization domain against measured minima of -7.7, clipping precisely the most informative nucleotides — a scientific error in the feature that justifies the whole architecture. And its archival leg drops the workbench and the NTScore, so the permanent artifact is strictly worse than [static]'s permanent artifact while the transient one costs 42 dev-days of a React stack the author cannot maintain. The right resolution is not to reject the workbench but to inverse its dependency: static primary, query tier optional and additive.

WHY [framework] IS THIRD AT 75. Intellectually the best-argued document of the four — the framework comparison is genuinely excellent and the Dash-renders-real-DOM insight is correct and load-bearing — and it caught a real silent-corruption bug (APEX1 gene-keyed slicing) that belongs in every build. But on scientific value it is dominated: it pays the full operational cost of a live server and collects almost none of the dividend, explicitly declining any set-query capability. It then compounds that by choosing a framework that concedes it has no force layout and no edge bundling for R3 — the view whose entire purpose is legible structure — and by autoscaling the NTScore y-axis per transcript, which quietly makes cross-gene comparison of the manuscript's central quantity invalid.

WHY [narrative] IS 2. Every field is the literal string "undefined". It is not a weak design; it is an absent one. Worth noting only that a genuine narrative angle — a guided path through the ZNF-artifact story — would have been the most persuasive thing this portal could offer a reviewer, and that possibility remains unexplored.

THE DECIDING CONSIDERATION. Two of the three real designs put a live process between a reader and the science. The measurements in the surveys make that unnecessary for everything R1/R2/R3 actually require: 1.13 ms per gene from a static shard, 33.9 MB for the full-resolution score tracks, 100 MB for the entire corpus. The server buys exactly one thing worth having — arbitrary set queries and on-the-fly enrichment — and that thing is separable. So the hybrid is static-core plus an optional, feature-detected query tier, with the two catalog units nobody built (mRNA projection, in-transcript coupling arcs) added to close the gap between "here are your gene's motifs" and "here is what they pair with, in your gene".

The per-line NTScore canvas strip above each 60-character line is the single best micro-detail in the whole set: it keeps the quantitative channel glued to the letters in read mode, which nobody else attempts. State discipline is the strictest of the four — every panel writes into the hash (#/gene/ACTB?r=utr3&pos=82&m=utr3_0313), so any view a reader reaches is a URL they can paste into a supplement, and every one of the 94 units declares its entry and exit routes, which is why the R1->R2->R3 chain actually closes instead of being asserted. Correct encoding discipline: motif fill is module-or-grey, never a 900-way cluster hash; cluster identity is pushed to label/selection/tooltip. Filters dim to 25% rather than removing, so motif density is never misrepresented and coordinates never shift. Three genuinely distinct, designed empty states (over-length transcript / missing region / no module) instead of blanks. The evidence page's raw-NPMI <-> gated toggle that animates 25 artifact rows falling away is the most persuasive single interaction proposed by anyone. For a portal whose second requirement is the cluster, that is a structural hole, not an omission. Second: the 519-node / 2,620-edge SVG force graph is the default 'full' mode with no matrix alternative and no hub-declutter control. Protein degree maxes at 62 and the top ten protein hubs carry 20.5% of all edges; a frozen bipartite layout mitigates but does not cure that, and the score slider only trades density for coverage. Third, and most substantively: R1 draws three disconnected axes. The projection cds = 3*protein + 3 holds in 19,210/19,210 rows, so protein motifs can be placed on the same nucleotide ruler as UTR motifs and the in-transcript coupling (median 2, mean 8.04 co-present gated pairs) can be drawn as arcs. Static shows the two languages side by side and never once shows them talking, which is the paper's entire claim. My lens is buildability and survival, so I weight three things: (1) how much of the deliverable is in a language and toolchain the author already commands, (2) whether the artifact keeps working with zero human attention, (3) whether the data volume actually fits the stated hosting.

On (3) the decisive fact is that [static] measured what nobody else did: uint8-quantized NTScore is 33.9 MB for the entire corpus, ~1.9 KB per transcript, at a vertical resolution finer than one screen pixel. Both server designs lean their primary justification on "288 MB of HDF5 cannot ship to a browser." It can.
